title: Show HN: Scolast – AI tutor for autodidacts inspired by Bloom's 2 sigma problem
text:
I was using Claude to learn physics and I was getting a bit frustrated with the interface (I kept interrupting the conversation to get a quick explainer on something, and there was no good interface for Claude to ask me questions) so I built Scolast!

It's an AI tutor that follows Bloom's findings (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bloom%27s_2_sigma_problem) that 1 to 1 tutoring, using mastery learning (basically only moving ahead when the student has demonstrated they learned something, but also moving ahead as quickly as possible) can have pretty incredible results, around two standard deviations higher than regular classroom learning. Bloom called it a problem because this was obviously untenable - but it's actually possible now!

I also added little side explainers for anything that's confusing, plus worksheets, and I've been iterating on the voice of the tutor, to try to get a sort of Feynman-y focus on the whys and the experiments and experiences that motivated each piece of knowledge.

I find that it's quite remarkable, I'm actually retaining some of the physics I've never been able to retain in the past, and it seems useful in a lot of other domains - my wife used it for language learning and to pass a yoga exam; I've used it to learn some machine learning subjects, etc. One interesting side effect is that I find using it quite tiring, and I actually use tokens very slowly compared to agentic coding - when you actually have to read every token carefully you really get your money's worth.

Would love to get people's thoughts so I'm throwing in $3 in free tokens while my budget lasts. After that you can buy tokens and I'm charging an extra 10% to cover everything else. Eventually I'd like to hook it up to people's existing subscriptions, I've applied to OAI's program for this, waiting to see if Ant will offer it.

Cheers

title: Re: Conker's Bad Fur Day (N64 US) 100% decompiled to b...
text:
This decompilation started in the summer from the original mkst/conker repository. All 2.25 MB of CPU code is matched and fully-linked. 97% is C. The other 2.8% is hand-written assembly (exception handlers, 64-bit math), and each piece has a recorded proof or search evidence that it was never C. About 80% of the functions have names. Game data is defined in C. The repo has no ROM and no assets.

Most of the work was done by fleets of Claude agents working in parallel. Each worked in its own workspace, and a change landed only if the whole ROM still matched. The project leans on deterministic checks to validate all work. CI rebuilds the ROM, checks that every function is either compiled C or proven hand-written asm, rejects any pointer written as a number, and caps compiler warnings.

I am very excited to reach this milestone. It was always one of my favorite games growing up.

title: Re: Show HN: Track people in video locally without AGP...
text:
Back in 2017 I wrote a small YOLOv2 + DeepSORT vision tracking repo that still gets occasional issues (I know, weird right). I finally rebuilt it from scratch on ONNX Runtime (well Claude did, but I asked him nicely to).

Browser demo: https://obendidi.github.io/trackflow/

This was what I strived to build in 2017 with much less success, because (1) I was a noob still learning the difference between concurrency and parallelism and (2) I didn't have a world class level coding assistant that doesn't know how to quit

Anyhow, anyone can use it locally without pulling in AGPL weights or cloud APIs. On small off-the-shelf models it beats Roboflow's trackers package across 81 DanceTrack, SportsMOT, MOT17, and MOT20 validation videos (charts in the README), and includes local video text search. Happy to have your feedback.

title: Re: AI Is Fire...
text:
> Before we harnessed the power of fire, we’d each spend many hours just chewing our food. This was needed to extract the calories we needed to hunt, gather, and procreate. Only when we started to cook food did we dramatically reduce the time it took to consume calories, increase the calories we consumed, and grow our brains.

A nitpick to be sure, but I imagine that it also greatly increase the range of things that are edible at all, and reduced our burden of bacteria and parasites.

> “AI should be banned from schools” is a strong opinion some have, but we rarely hear “Computer software should be banned from schools”. This is due to this narrow view of what it is and it mirrors our ancestors’ naive, but understandable, opinion that “fire bad!“.

This is uncharitable to the critics. Before the ubiquity of the Internet, the most obvious way to use a computer to "cheat" at school is as a more powerful calculator; the same arguments apply as for an actual calculator, where you need to know what buttons to push, how to analyze a problem. And on the teaching side, how to pose a problem where the calculation itself isn't the interesting part. (And we do still expect young children to learn arithmetic.) The software we allow in the computer lab can be chosen and made fit for purpose. (And a phone arguably is a "computer" running its own "software", and people do call to ban them from schools, for a variety of reasons.) On the other hand, AI purports to do the analysis for you and to be general-purpose; and the easiest and most obvious way that students would use it in a school environment is pretty clearly a) cheating and b) defeating the purpose of pretty much any problem I could imagine a teacher posing, unless the problem is specifically about learning how to use AI (which is intuitive enough already thanks to ChatGPT and, I suppose, voice transcription).

> Turning off the supply of energy seems easy enough, since we can just unplug it, but when compute is spread over the planet and is controlled by many different invested parties, it’s not so easy.

Sure, but we don't have to assume a pressing need to keep developing AI capabilities. The underlying premise is, seemingly, that national defense requires staying ahead of the other guys (who are simultaneously imagined to not really be able to do much of their own novel development and mainly keep up by doing "distillation"). I'm not really sold on that. The game theory of nuclear warfare doesn't seem to have required nearly as many warheads as were actually developed, either.

> Don’t explore a dry forest in a lightning storm, don’t show your kids how to access the dark web, and don’t say “Surprise me!” to an AI that has access to your bank accounts.

I don't disagree, but this seems rather incongruous with the previous point. One can imagine a future where someone else's AI has access to your bank accounts, and it's out of your control (the bank's fault). There are multiple possible paths to that even if we do find out that our cryptographic algorithms are indeed as secure as they were designed to be.

title: Re: Catching Gemini 4's leaking thought summarizer mid...
text:
Author here. I was having a lot of fun playing with Gemini 4 Neon. I must say I've been rather pleasantly surprised with its performance and it's become a daily driver for me at high and extra high. Besides being a good coding agent, I've really enjoyed its personality too. Coding with a coding agent all day can be a little flat, so when it reciprocates banter or feels more like a coding colleague than something flat like a Sol or Astra model, I was pleased to see that.

I also noticed its chain of thought messages had a funny, overly clinical tone to them. e.g.:

> Me: you have [home assistant] mcp right

> Neon (CoT): Environment tool configuration indicates specific capabilities available across domains, though parsing restrictions require verifying operational constraints before proceeding with target integrations.

All this to say, I was paying closer attention to the chain of thought messages when I noticed some seemingly unrelated stuff around port bindings and database latency in the thought trace while it was answering a question about Sweetwater candy of all things. So naturally I grepped ~13,000 local thoughts from the past week and there were a few interesting finds, including some of the chain of thought summarizer prompt leaking through as well as catching Google mid-rollout of a new version of their chain of thought summarizer around 21:00 UTC yesterday. Happy to share more logs if anyone's curious, though I suspect you can grep this in your own as well.

title: Re: We built self-improving AI agents for customer ser...
text:
Hi, I'm the founder of Aide (https://aide.app), we've been building in the customer service space since GPT-3 was in beta, and the holy grail ever was always building agents that learn from conversations and automatically update their configuration. The question we kept asking ourselves is how can we build AI agents to continuously improve to eventually get as good as human agents? The solution we landed on involves reviewing conversations, learning from them, diffing what it learned against its current configuration, while ALSO scoring human agent conversations and holding the AI agent's responses to the same bar. Tracking the impact of learnings and changes on support metrics and KPIs was also a key factor in this process.

Figured this would be relevant to share since building self-improving is top of mind for most agentic teams and a lot of what we built here can be helpful to teams looking for inspiration or similar solutions!
